full_judgment:
4. The defence of the defendant no. 1 in both the suits was that, he was a watchman of the plaintiff. The suit land in T.S No. 76/58 was leased out to him by Mr. Hithford, the then Manager of the plaintiff Company at the rate of Re. 1 per bigas per year 31/32 years back. He has possessed the suit land as a tenant paying rent thereof. He has acquired tenancy right in the suit land and is not liable to be evicted. He denied execution of any license document. He hold the homestead which is the subject matter of T.S. No. 98/58 as nonkar tenant as he rendered services to the plaintiff. He built all the huts in question at his own cost. After the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 he held the land as tenant under the Government. He is, therefore, not liable to be evicted. The defendant No. 2, the then Government of East Pakistan entered appearance but did not contest the suits. 

 10. The appellate Court then found that the defendant no.1 has been in possession of the suit land for the last 25/26 years. It found that the defendant no. 1 has been described as a tenant and the amount paid by him has been described as rent in Ext. 3, a rent record book, in Exts. C, C(1) and C(2), counterfoils of rent receipts and in Ext. A-A(5), the rent-receipts. The counterfoils and rent-receipts are forms of receipt maintained under rule 75 of section 72 of the Sylhet Tenancy Act, 1936 which strongly suggest a tenancy. Further, in the plaint itself the transaction in question has been described as a lease in more than one place. The appellate Court below then noticed some of the provisions of the agreement in question Ext. 1(c). In clause I thereof the defendants was authorised "to hold" the set it land. The appellate Court interpreted the word "hold" to mean occupation and keeping possession of the suit land. The words used in the document, according to the appellate Court, indicate that a lease was granted to the defendant. The uninterrupted possession of the suit land for the last 25 years suggests that the defendant was given exclusive possession of the suit land. There is no evidence on record that the plaintiff ever executed any act of ownership over the suit land during the period in which the defendant was in possession of it the defendant's exclusive possession suggest a lease. The plaintiff took the plea that the suit land, admittedly situated within the tea estate itself, cannot be leased out. Under the Explanation to section 1 of the Sylhet Tenancy Act, 1936 land included in a tea estate is excluded from the operation of the said Act if it is let out for the maintenance of the coolies working on the cultivation. The plaintiff pleaded that the defendant No. 1 was a coolie and the suit land was licensed out to him for his maintenance. The appellate Court held that the Sylhet Tenancy Act, 1936 applies to the suit land because the defendant No. 1 was not a coolie but a chowkidar. With the coming into force of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 the rent-receiving interest of the plaintiff in the suit land was acquired by the Government and the defendant No. 1 holds the suit land under the Government as a tenant. The defendant therefore cannot be evicted.
